evidence: The W ALD film growth is accomplished by two self-limiting surface reactions that have been described in previous work: (A) WF3⁎ + Si2H6→W–SiH⁎ + SiHF3 + 2H2 (1) (B) WSiH⁎ + WF6→W–WF3⁎ + SiHF3 (2) where the asterisks denote the surface species. The W ALD growth occurs during alternating exposures to WF6 and Si2H6. By repeating the surface reactions given by Eqs. (1) and (2), W ALD growth occurs very linearly with the number of AB cycles. The measured W ALD growth rates typically range from 4.0 – 6.0 Å per AB cycle depending on temperature. Although the W ALD films are polycrystalline, they are very smooth and conformal to the underlying substrate. W ALD can be performed over a wide range of temperatures from 30 –325 °C. The lower temperatures in this range are low enough to allow W ALD to be performed on polymer substrates. Consequently, W ALD can deposit a metallic and conducting film on polymer films or polymer particles. W ALD films on polymers may be useful for electromagnetic interference shielding on polymer-packaged devices. Because tungsten is a hard refractive metal, W ALD may be useful to strengthen polymer films or polymer particles. Continuous W ALD films may also provide gas diffusion barrier properties. Since tungsten is a reasonable reflector, W ALD may be useful to deposit flexible mirrors on polymers.
